name: SIGMA - SSH Session Cadence Brute-Force Indicator (Zeek ssh.log) [threshold]
description: Elastic threshold companion for rules/sigma/net_zeek_ssh_session_cadence.yml (issue #332, found during #261's security-auditor review). Alerts when a single source (source.ip) establishes >=5 SSH sessions (event.dataset:zeek.ssh, any client version-exchange banner Zeek parsed) within a 10-minute lookback (the real trigger is 5-in-10, not 5-in-5 - see the from/interval overlap note below). Reads zeek.ssh session records directly rather than the aggregated notice.log SSH::Password_Guessing/Login_By_Password_Guesser detect-bruteforcing.zeek fires on (30 failed auths / 30 minutes, both upstream Zeek defaults) - complementary coverage for the recall gap below that threshold, not a replacement for it. HONEST FRAMING (security-auditor finding): 5-in-10-minutes and 30-in-30-minutes are the SAME steady-state rate (~1 session/minute) - this rule improves DETECTION LATENCY for a burst-shaped attack and drops the dependency on auth_success, but does not lower the sustained rate an attacker can stay under to evade both rules indefinitely; a genuinely lower-rate long-window companion is a distinct, separate piece of work. Deliberately does not depend on auth_success: live-verified (client and server on separate docker network namespaces over a real bridge network, not loopback) that Zeek's auth_success field is entirely absent (not false) on failed-auth ssh.log records - tests/anomaly_simulation/verify_detections.py's own comment documents this same unreliability specifically over loopback (large MTU defeats Zeek's packet-size auth-outcome heuristic); this rule's own verification independently reproduced the identical symptom over a different topology. The Sigma file is the documented logic-of-record (single-session definition, including a documented known-limitation note on SSH::Info$client being &optional on a lossy capture vantage); this threshold rule adds the per-source count that sigma_eval.py / the lucene conversion target cannot express. security-auditor review (#393, FIXED not deferred): the original "from": "now-6m" (flat +1-minute overlap over the 5-minute "interval") was mathematically incomplete - a real sliding 5-6-minute window is fully contained in a single 6-minute run window only when its start falls in a 1-minute band out of every 5 (20% containment probability for an arbitrary-phase campaign - the same math #392's own review independently confirmed for the sustained-cadence sibling rule, where the effect was far more severe at a wider window). Corrected to "from": "now-10m" (lookback >= interval + the 5-minute detection window), which GUARANTEES full containment for any campaign phase. This is the fix auth-win-bruteforce-failed-logons.ndjson's own description previously deferred as a shared follow-up - both files are fixed together in this same change, not one-sided. Cost: the effective counting window widens from 6 to 10 minutes and duplicate-alert risk across overlapping runs is not independently verified against multiple real Kibana scheduled runs. Reads zeek.ssh, a genuinely different dataset than the pipeline's zeek.notice-driven T1110 tag, so neither path double-counts the same document - but a single high-volume attack can legitimately trip both, and metric_raw_alert_volume() sums its two sub-counts into one combined value even though it reports them separately too. This rule's alerts are NOT wired to SOAR dispatch (the /alert trigger gates on a threat.technique.id the zeek.notice path sets, not this one) - do not close that gap by tagging threat.technique.id on zeek.ssh documents directly, which would fire the unrate-limited /alert webhook once per real SSH session. KNOWN GAP (see the Sigma file's own description): a per-source.ip threshold cannot catch a genuinely distributed attack (many sources, each individually under threshold) - out of scope for this rule, tracked as a distinct piece of work.
author: Suburban-SOC
false_positives: An admin or automation tool (Ansible, deployment scripts, health checks) establishing several sequential SSH connections to the same host within a short window - legitimate session-reconnect patterns can resemble low-volume brute-force cadence at this threshold.
A jump host or bastion legitimately proxying multiple real users' sessions from one apparent source IP.
